claims.text: Friction stir processing can repair localized surface damage in high-value components.
Friction stir processing produces a refined, solid-state reconditioned surface.
FSP-treated surfaces have greater hardness than conventional fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
FSP-treated surfaces have greater wear resistance than conventional fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
FSP-treated surfaces have greater corrosion resistance than conventional fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
FSP reduces susceptibility to hot cracking relative to conventional fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
FSP must generate sufficient localized plastic deformation while maintaining the peak temperature below the substrate melting point.
The proposed treatment is suitable only for components that can tolerate the mechanical deformation imposed by FSP.
FSP creates a refined, recrystallized surface microstructure with reduced grain size.
FSP enhances compressive residual stresses at the processed surface.
Intense plastic deformation during FSP causes grain refinement and homogenization of the surface layer.
The refined and homogenized surface layer increases local hardness.
Compressive residual stress and increased local hardness jointly mitigate crack initiation, especially hot cracking.
Grain refinement, homogenization, compressive residual stress, and increased hardness improve wear resistance.
Grain refinement, homogenization, compressive residual stress, and increased hardness improve corrosion resistance.
The expected performance benefits are particularly relevant under aggressive wear, corrosive-media, and thermal-stress conditions.
The intervention requires an accessible, locally repairable region and sufficient substrate thickness to withstand processing without loss of integrity.
FSP may be unsuitable for very intricate geometries.
FSP may be unsuitable where mechanical loading prevents tight control of induced stresses.
